note.explanation: Acid rain forms when oxides of sulphur and nitrogen mix with moisture in the air. For example, SO₃ reacts with water to make H₂SO₄, while NO₂ reacts with water to make HNO₃ and HNO₂. Acid rain can harm soil, plants, aquatic life, human health, agriculture and human-made structures.
note.simple: Acid rain is rain containing acids made from gases in the air. It can damage living things and structures.

examTips: Acid rain can be tested as a short-answer definition or as a question asking for its causes and effects.
For the pH question, give the textbook range exactly: 4.2 to 4.4.
For formation questions, show the relevant balanced equations and name the acids: H₂SO₄, HNO₃ and HNO₂.
For an effects question, identify the affected area—such as soil, plants, aquatic life or structures—and explain the damage.
In marking, correct equations, accurate chemical formulae and clear cause-and-effect statements earn marks; do not give only a list of effects when an explanation is asked.

explain.title: What acid rain means
explain.body: When rain water has pH between 4.2 and 4.4, it is known as acid rain. Learn this range exactly for a definition or short-answer question.

explain.title: How acid rain forms
explain.body: Burning fossil fuels releases SO₂. In the atmosphere, SO₂ can be converted to SO₃, which reacts with water to form H₂SO₄. Nitrogen oxides also react with water: 2NO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HNO₃(g) + HNO₂(g). The acids form droplets that can be carried far by wind before falling as rain, hail, snow or fog.

explain.title: Effects of acid rain
explain.body: Acid rain makes soil more acidic and washes away nutrients. It can damage plants and forests, make water too acidic for aquatic animals, and contribute to harm from toxic substances leached from soil. It also damages crops and human-made structures such as buildings, statues, automobiles and bridges.

explain.title: Reducing agricultural damage
explain.body: Farmers can monitor soil conditions and, when necessary, add crushed lime (CaO) to neutralize acid.

mistakes: Do not give a pH range other than 4.2–4.4 when using the textbook definition.
Do not confuse the gases with the acids: SO₂ and NO₂ are oxides; H₂SO₄, HNO₃ and HNO₂ are acids.
Do not leave out HNO₂ when writing the products of the nitrogen-dioxide reaction with water.
Do not say that acid rain only harms plants; it can also affect soil, aquatic life, human health, agriculture and structures.
When explaining the effect on soil after trees are destroyed, include that soil is washed away and new plants cannot grow there.
